title: Wickham Cuffee
summary: Wickham Cuffee (1826–1915) was a Shinnecock whaler, navigator, trustee, Presbyterian elder, basketmaker, farmer, and keeper of family and community knowledge.
content:
Wickham Cuffee (1826–1915) was a Shinnecock whaler, navigator, trustee, Presbyterian elder, basketmaker, farmer, and keeper of family and community knowledge. His long life crossed the era of deep-sea whaling, the 1859 loss of Shinnecock Hills lease rights, and the period when outside researchers came to the reservation seeking language and architectural knowledge.1

Family and Shinnecock roots

Born on the Shinnecock Reservation in 1826, Wickham was the son of Vincent Cuffee and Sarah Bunn. His daughter Lulu Elisa Cuffee married Charles Sylvester Hunter, and their daughter Lois Marie Hunter—later known as Princess Nowedonah—preserved much of her grandfather’s story in Shinnecock-authored history.2

Whaling and navigation

As a young man, Wickham joined the maritime economy in which Shinnecock workers served as whalers, sailors, boatsteerers, mates, and navigators. Sources remember him by the nickname “Eagle Eye” for his ability to spot whale spouts at a distance. Hunter also preserved a family account that he navigated a whaling vessel home after its captain died during an Arctic voyage. The voyage detail should be read as family history while crew records remain to be identified.3

Trusteeship and the 1859 deed

Wickham served as a Shinnecock trustee. On April 21, 1859, he, Stephen H. Walker, and David S. Bunn appeared before Southampton Town Clerk Charles Howell to acknowledge their signatures on the deed associated with the loss of Shinnecock Hills lease rights. A signature in a colonial legal record does not by itself prove equal power or community consent; the transaction belongs within the broader history of land pressure, contested authority, and Shinnecock survival.4

Language, architecture, and teaching

By the early twentieth century, Wickham was one of the Shinnecock elders whom researchers approached about language and older building practices. Lois Marie Hunter wrote that he remembered the last wigwam used as a residence and helped explain its construction. He made a model for M. R. Harrington in 1902. The resulting record preserves knowledge, but it should also be read critically because museums and anthropologists often extracted Native knowledge while imposing their own ideas about authenticity and disappearance.5

Later years

Hunter remembered her grandfather making white-oak splint baskets and scrubs in his later years. Around age eighty he recovered from a broken hip with help from Southampton physician George H. Schenck, and the two exchanged stories about Wickham’s voyages. A 1909 state health report also included his photograph, which newspapers used to compare his appearance to George Washington. Wickham died in 1915 at eighty-nine.6

Reading the record carefully

Outside writers repeatedly called Wickham the “last” Shinnecock or treated him as a remnant of a disappearing people. That framing was false. His work, family, trusteeship, language knowledge, craft, church life, and descendants show continued Shinnecock community life. The nickname story connecting “Wickham” to “wickiup” is best presented as family tradition, not settled linguistic evidence.

References

  • Lois Marie Hunter, The Shinnecock Indians (Buys Bros., 1950), PDF pp. 2–3, 24, 33–34, and 46.
  • Gaynell Stone, ed., The Shinnecock Indians: A Culture History (1983), pp. 267, 301, 304, 307, 310, and 318–319.
  • Beverly Jensen, Shinnecock Indian Nation (2015), pp. 195–198.
  • Sandi Brewster-Walker, Long Island Native American family genealogy (2008), p. 521.
  • Nomi Dayan, Whaling on Long Island (2016), p. 349.
why_this_matters: Wickham Cuffee’s biography connects Shinnecock maritime expertise, land governance, language and architectural knowledge, craft, church life, and family memory while directly rejecting the false ‘last Indian’ framing imposed by outside writers.
activity_update_summary: Expanded Wickham Cuffee’s biography with sourced whaling, trusteeship, language, architecture, craft, family history, and mapped Historic Moments.
